subdivision.heading: Joining and Separating Claims and Parties

operative_text.controlling:
3.70(1)  Two or more parties may join to bring an action, and a
plaintiff or originating applicant may make a claim against 2 or
more persons as defendants or respondents in an action, if
(a) the claim arises out of the same transaction or occurrence
or series of transactions or occurrences,
(b) a question of law or fact common to the parties is likely to
arise, or
(c) the Court permits.
(2)  This rule applies irrespective of the remedy claimed by the
plaintiff or originating applicant and whether or not 2 or more
plaintiffs or originating applicants seek the same remedy.

BOOK_A.related_provisions: 2.6 (representative actions);12.5 (non-spouse parties in family litigation). See also R.2.6 (representative actions) and R.2.9 (class actions). Generally speaking, the same person cannot be both plaintiff and defendant (even in representative capacities).R.2.2(2) on overlapping partnerships is an exception. One cannot get judgment against a non-party, e.g.a mere"third party by order"under the Insurance Act. Rule 3.70 is broadly construed in the light of the severance power.Rule 3.70 is ordinarily satisfied if there is a common question of law or fact. The power to add new causes of action may be narrower than the power to join them in the first place. Who is a party or not is very important, for it governs who has a right to notice and to make applications or participate in applications or the trial.Generally anin personamclaim can lead only to a judgment against a party, not a non-party.It is usually improper to take steps without notice to all parties, e.g.to get a "consent"order affecting a party, without telling the applications judge or judge that that party has not consented or even got notice. The court should avoid prejudice such as lack of a chance to lead evidence or argument against the proposed judgment. The courts cannot find statutes to be unconstitutional without advance notice to the relevant Attorneys General and a chance for them to argue the point. Where the Court of Appeal had raised the notice issue of its own motion, the decision is at least voidable, maybe even void. Defendants liable in the alternative or jointly can be joined in one suit. Usually all parties to a contract must be parties to a suit about it, unless full adjudication and justice without all parties is possible. The court cannot rectify a contract unless all the parties to the contract are before the court.A counterclaim was stayed until that was done. The extraction interleaves the columns and footnotes on pp.3-224 and 3-225 so that many sentences are split across non-adjacent lines (e.g. 'An order should not be made' at line 7273 is completed by 'against the Legal Aid Society ...' at line 7278; 'Where a party abandoned all its rights ... it should' at line 7301 is completed by 'get itself removed as a party' at line 7307); the wording is kept as printed. (1) Related Provisions: '2.6 (representative actions)' agrees with the official title of 2.6 ('Representative actions'); '12.5 (non-spouse parties in family litigation)' (official 12.5 'Requirement that parties be spouses' - a paraphrase); 'See also R.2.6 (representative actions) and R.2.9 (class actions)' (official 2.9 'Class proceedings practice and procedure'). (2) Statements read against the official text: 'R.2.2(2) on overlapping partnerships is an exception' to the rule that the same person cannot be plaintiff and defendant agrees with official 2.2(2) ('an action between partnerships having one or more partners in common'); 'Rule 3.70 is ordinarily satisfied if there is a common question of law or fact' agrees with 3.70(1)(b) and Book B's part 1 (Pockar Brothers, 'a common factor of law or fact may give rise to the right to have actions joined'); 'Defendants liable in the alternative or jointly can be joined in one suit' agrees with 3.70(1)(a)-(b) and 3.69(3); 'Rule 3.70 is broadly construed in the light of the severance power' (3.71) is not in the Rules; 'The power to add new causes of action may be narrower than the power to join them' has no rule cited. commentary.text: Rule 3.70 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 3.70. It will be noted that in dealing with the question of misjoinder R. 36 uses the test set out in the following words, “in respect of or arising out of the same transaction or occurrence”… … a common factor of law or fact may give rise to the right to have actions joined for purposes of the proceedings. Pockar Brothers Masonry Ltd. v. Hilberta Construction Co. (1978), 6 Alta. L.R. (2d) 289 at 291 (C.A.).
